Das Gameplay fühlt sich sehr eintönig und repetitiv an. Man läuft durch Level, haut auf Gegner ein, bekommt ein paar Combos und Effekte geboten und genau das wiederholt sich dann über Stunden. Es fehlt an wirklicher Tiefe, Abwechslung und spannenden Mechaniken, die einen wirklich motivieren weiterzuspielen. Schnell hat man das Gefühl, immer wieder das gleiche Muster zu durchlaufen.

Auch die Gegnergestaltung bleibt für mich enttäuschend. Viele Feinde wirken wie Copy Paste Varianten derselben Gegner mit etwas abgewandelten Stats oder Farben, es gibt kaum echte Überraschungen oder besondere Kampfbegegnungen, die hängen bleiben.

Technisch und grafisch wirkt das Spiel nicht mehr zeitgemäß. Effekte und Animationen sehen grauenhaft aus und stellenweise hapert es an Animationen oder Treffereffekten, die eigentlich einem Hack and Slash Titel mehr Wucht und Feedback geben sollten.

Die Story ist sehr dünn und lässt einen schnell kalt, selbst wenn man die Serie kennt. Für Neueinsteiger ins RWBY Universum ist sie kaum zugänglich und für Fans bietet sie kaum wirklichen Mehrwert, viel passiert nicht, vieles passiert ohne große Emotion oder Dramaturgie.

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is a cooperative-focused action game that translates the energy, style, and character-driven appeal of the RWBY animated series into a playable hack-and-slash experience. Developed by Rooster Teeth Games in collaboration with FarBridge and published by FarBridge, the game represents an official expansion of the RWBY universe rather than a retelling of existing episodes. It is designed first and foremost as a fan-facing title, aiming to capture the rhythm of team-based combat against hordes of Grimm while offering a light narrative that fits comfortably within the show’s canon timeline.

Set between the second and third volumes of the animated series, the story follows Team RWBY as they investigate strange Grimm behavior and uncover the machinations of a new antagonist, Doctor Merlot. The narrative is straightforward and largely serves as a framework to move players through a series of combat-driven missions, but it succeeds in reinforcing the personalities and relationships of the core cast. Dialogue, banter, and voice performances—delivered by the original voice actors—help maintain continuity with the show, making the experience feel like an interactive side story rather than a disconnected spin-off.

Gameplay centers on third-person hack-and-slash combat, with players choosing from multiple characters, each equipped with their signature weapons and unique fighting styles. Characters such as Ruby, Weiss, Blake, and Yang all feel distinct in how they move, attack, and manage crowd control, encouraging experimentation and replay. Combat emphasizes fast movement, basic combo chains, dodging, and special abilities, keeping encounters accessible and easy to understand even for players unfamiliar with action games. While the mechanics are not especially complex, they are responsive and enjoyable, particularly when enemies swarm the screen and teamwork becomes essential.

The game is clearly built with cooperative play in mind, supporting up to four players online. In co-op, RWBY: Grimm Eclipse shines the brightest, as shared combat encounters become more dynamic and chaotic. Players can revive one another, coordinate abilities, and divide attention between enemy groups, making battles feel more engaging than in solo play. Horde-style modes, where teams defend areas against escalating waves of Grimm, are especially effective at showcasing this design focus, offering repeatable challenges that reward coordination and familiarity with character kits.

Progression is handled through experience points, skill upgrades, and unlockable perks that enhance each character’s abilities. While the progression system is relatively shallow compared to deeper action RPGs, it provides enough customization to encourage continued play. Players can fine-tune stats, unlock new moves, and experiment with different builds, though the impact of these upgrades remains modest. The emphasis remains on moment-to-moment action rather than long-term character optimization.

Visually, RWBY: Grimm Eclipse adopts a stylized aesthetic that closely mirrors the look of the animated series. Character models are instantly recognizable, and combat effects—such as weapon trails and elemental attacks—add flair to encounters. Environments draw inspiration from familiar locations in the RWBY world, though level layouts are often linear and reused across missions. While the visuals are serviceable and appealing to fans, they lack the environmental depth or variety found in higher-budget action titles, occasionally contributing to a sense of repetition over extended sessions.

Enemy design primarily revolves around different Grimm types, each with slightly varied behaviors and attack patterns. While some enemies introduce mild tactical considerations, overall enemy variety is limited, and combat scenarios often rely on increasing enemy numbers rather than introducing fundamentally new challenges. Boss encounters offer brief spikes in intensity but tend to follow predictable patterns, reinforcing the game’s accessible, arcade-like nature.

One of the game’s most notable strengths is its tone. RWBY: Grimm Eclipse does not attempt to be overly serious or mechanically demanding, instead focusing on delivering an enjoyable, character-driven experience that complements its source material. This approach makes it approachable for a wide audience, including players who may primarily be fans of the show rather than action game enthusiasts. At the same time, this design philosophy is also its main weakness, as players seeking deep combat systems or extensive content may find the experience lacking in long-term depth.

Overall, RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is best understood as a cooperative action game built around fan service, accessibility, and teamwork rather than innovation or complexity. It succeeds in bringing Team RWBY into an interactive format that feels authentic and enjoyable when played with others, even if its mechanics and content remain relatively modest. For fans of the RWBY franchise or players looking for a light, co-op hack-and-slash experience, it offers an entertaining way to step into the world of Remnant and battle Grimm alongside friends.

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is a straightforward co-op action game that’s clearly made for fans of the show first and everyone else second. It drops you into missions where you fight waves of Grimm, clear objectives, and move through areas that feel like they were built to recreate RWBY’s vibe more than to be complex arenas.

Combat is simple and very readable. Each character has their own weapon style and a few abilities, so the basics are easy to understand: light/heavy attacks, dodges, and skill cooldowns. When the game flows, it’s satisfying to string hits together and clear a room quickly, especially with teammates covering different angles.

Co-op is where it’s at. With friends, the game becomes a lot more fun because you can coordinate, revive each other, and keep the pace moving. Solo play works, but it’s noticeably less exciting since the missions are designed around the energy of a group pushing forward together.

Progression is mostly about leveling up and improving your skills. It gives you a reason to replay missions, try different characters, and slowly feel stronger. It’s not deep in a “build-crafting” way, but it’s enough to create a sense of growth as you unlock upgrades and get more comfortable with timing and positioning.

Level design is mixed. Some stages feel like a clean run from fight to fight, while others feel repetitive with similar corridors, repeated enemy waves, and objectives that don’t change much. Enemy variety also isn’t huge, so the game leans on higher difficulty and bigger swarms to keep things tense.

Presentation is very “RWBY,” which is a plus if you’re into the series. The characters, effects, and overall style match the source material, even if the game itself looks a bit dated. Audio and voice work help sell the atmosphere, and the soundtrack keeps a decent pace during longer sessions.

Overall, RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is best as a casual co-op game for fans who want to play as the team and beat up Grimm with friends. If you’re expecting a deep action system or tons of variety, it may feel repetitive fast, but if you want a light, mission-based brawler with RWBY flavor, it does the job.

I REALLY wanted to like this game because to tell you the truth, I actually use to be really into RWBY at one point. It’s a really fun show with great characters, music, action and is just one of those things I think has a lot of good to it. So when I saw that there was an actual RWBY game back in the day which was actually made by Roster Teath themselves, had all of the voice actors from the show voice in it AND was a co op hack and slash I HAD to give this a try… And I had really mixed feelings of it and playing this game again recently only reminded me why I feel out of it originally.

And most of my issues come down to the actual gameplay. You got a basic three hit light attack combo, a heavy attack, ranged attack, counter attacks and… that’s it. Oh but you can level up each character and new skills for them… And it’s only for there ranged attacks, ultimates, team attacks and general skills. No new moves or anything. The combos you start with is all you get and outside of the speed and some animation changes it’s the same core combat across all four of the girls with the only thing that’s different between them of note is there ultimates and ranged attacks. The DLC characters DO have more unique skill tress but it still doesn’t fix my main issue with the gameplay. I mean come on, this is RWBY we are talking about! A show that has some intense action to it and characters who pull off some of the most insane attacks and physics defying ♥♥♥♥ ever, yet all we get is really basic attacks. I’m not expecting it to be Devil May Cry or Bayonetta levels of gameplay but I do at least expect a little more than this. Although now that I think about, a RWBY game with Devil May Cry or Bayonetta or styled gameplay would be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome. Because this feels to basic to me which normally I don’t mind basic gameplay but even in games like Hyrule Warriors or the LEGO games there’s still WAY more going on in what your doing in the levels themselves but in this game the most variety it has, if we can even call it that, is just defending an objective agents waves or Grimm or finding collectables for more EXP.

But that’s not even the worst of it because if you dare make the mistake of playing this game by yourself in single player you are going to learn quickly that this game is NOT designed around single player at all. Not only does pausing the game in single player mode NOT actually pause the action around you and just brings up the menu which is already an unbearable decision anyway because what if someone’s calling me or I need to go to the bathroom but the enemies in just the FIRST LEVEL alone on NORMAL DIFFICUTLY can kill you in only a few hits! I’m not even kidding when I say the enemies early on feel like the kind of ones you’d face towards the end of the game, not right at the start when you likely would be starting out with no skills. And yeah, this is intended as a co op game, I get that, but even in games like Borderlands which are also intended to be played in Co Op it’s still balances itself around if you’re playing by yourself with lower enemy counts and you know, ACTUALLY LETTING YOU PAUSE THE ACTION! Pair this with the aforementioned combat and gameplay which get old really quickly and it feels more like a game that’s still in beta.

Yeah, despite my love for the show I’m not the biggest fan of this game. From the disappointing gameplay to how it almost feels like it punishes you for not having friends to play with. There is a chance playing this with friends is a lot better and when I did play this with other people a few years ago I did still have some fun with it but considering you can get other co op games on Steam like the aforementioned Borderlands, Left 4 Dead, Payday, Dead Island, Dying Light and a bunch of others which have way more going on in them, have a lot more polish to them and are a lot more single player friendly even you’re a die hard RWBY Fan I still wouldn’t recommend this.

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is not particularly polished or fun as a Hack-and-Slash, the story isn't that interesting and the graphics are low quality but knowing that this originally was an indie fan work officially supported by show creators gives it a bit of slack. 

If you're a RWBY fan, you will have a fun time for a run or two but otherwise it is repetitive and hollow. This game's fan base is dead unless you can pressure your friends into buying and playing it with you. Horde and Gauntlet (multiplayer modes) are mostly unplayable as a result, which by proxy makes collecting all of the achievements impossible. Not to mention they require that you at least purchase the DLC for JNPR, which I thought gave the game a little bit extra replay value but it should have been added by default. 

It does make for a good casual experience though, you can get through the campaign without much thought and I appreciate that the game is built in a way that you can always play multiplayer without fear of the servers getting shut down (P2P multiplayer). Bad news with that is every instance you play of the game is always considered "live" and pausing does not actually stop the game even in solo campaign, you can die while paused.

Play it if you want to, just get it on sale if you do.

Before I even write anything, let it be said first that if you do plan on buying this to be careful. Given the whole situation with Rooster Teeth's ownership moving around I have no idea who is getting the money for any of these purchases. So if you are concerned with where your money goes, definitely hold off on this.

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is... not a very good game. The levels are barren and simple. The fighting is also barren and simple- just a few combos with small variations between characters with the same goal of dealing damage. The story is not very good and very short (10 total missions with little substance in them).  The extra modes are also not very good. The leveling system for characters is pretty bad. Overall, just kind of a mediocre experience.

Despite that though, as a fan of RWBY back when it was airing in the good ol' days, there is a bit of charm to this. Sure the voice acting is bad, but it's the same VAs from those early seasons clearly trying their best (And that other guy is here too, which I would love to figure out how to mod him out iykyk). The story isn't good but it at least feels similar to some early season episodes. The combat could never live up to the show but it definitely feels like it tries. And I have to at least give it a smidge of credit for trying, especially for when this came out.

Also, playing with your friends is kind of fun. The leveling system is really frustrating and I can imagine it being very bad on games with more than 2 people, but it can also be funny when you bully your friends out of leveling up. I also really don't like that at least 6 achievements are locked behind a $5 dlc that 4 total people need to buy, but that's not really something that can be fixed right now I guess. Really this can just be an excuse to get some friends together for like 2 hours to mess around with, even if it's not the best thing you could be doing with your time.

So no, I wouldn't recommend this to your average joe. There are much, much better beat em' ups on the market right now. But, if you have a younger sibling that just learned about RWBY for the first time? This might be a cute thing to do together with them to show them a little piece of history.
